name: Natural Foot Society (Tianzu Hui)

image.caption: Manifesto of the Natural Foot Society by N̂g Gio̍k-kai

lead: The Natural Foot Society (Tian Zu Hui) was founded in Shanghai in 1895 to end foot binding, the practice of breaking and binding girls' feet to achieve tiny "lotus" feet, then a mark of beauty and marriage prospects. Its work is a case study in changing a beauty standard.
It used lectures, pamphlets and name lists, reached upper-class Chinese women, and emphasised health. Foot binding was banned in 1912 and had largely vanished by 1949.

paras: Members campaigned through talks, publications, pledges and petitions, including one to Empress Dowager Cixi.
The society documents a practice with severe harms: broken bones, infection and lasting disability.

chain: Campaign shifts foot binding from ideal to harm
angle.text: The society illustrates how a beauty standard can be changed through argument and social organising. It is historical context rather than a technique.

lead: The Natural Foot Society, or Tian Zu Hui, was founded in Shanghai in 1895 by ten women of different nationalities, led by Alicia Little, and is described as the first secular mass organisation against foot binding in China.[1]

Foot binding was a beauty ideal in late imperial China: the "golden lotus" foot of about 10-11 cm signified femininity and status and affected marriage prospects.[2] The society reframed natural feet as the healthy standard, arguing on health grounds rather than religion.[1]
Foot binding was banned in 1912, and the practice had largely disappeared by 1949.[1][2]
infobox: Alicia Little and nine other women

paras: Earlier groups such as the 1874 Heavenly Foot Society in Xiamen operated mainly within Christian missionary networks.[2] The 1895 society welcomed all religions and nationalities, targeted non-Christian Chinese elites and highlighted health problems.[1] It ran lecture tours and pamphlets, kept name lists, and petitioned Empress Dowager Cixi, who issued a ban in 1902 that could not be enforced.[1]

It became a national umbrella with local branches; in 1907 the Western founders handed leadership to Chinese women.[1] Reformers such as Kang Youwei, who founded a society near Canton in 1883, mainly argued about health and national strength.[2] Foot binding was banned in 1912, though enforcement was uneven.[2]
Binding broke the foot bones and folded the toes; reported results included infection, gangrene and lasting mobility problems, with estimates that up to 10% of girls died from complications.[2]

timeline.event: Heavenly Foot Society formed in Xiamen.[2]
Natural Foot Society founded in Shanghai.[1]
